chunks: First, conductive coupling through a shared impedance: two circuits share a ground or supply path, so one circuit's current creates a voltage drop that the other sees.
A classic is a digital return current flowing through the same ground trace as an analog reference. The voltage is I times Z, or L di/dt. Second, capacitive coupling.
Any two conductors have a mutual capacitance, and a changing voltage on one injects a current of C dv/dt into the other. It matters most for high-impedance victims.
Third, inductive coupling. Two current loops share magnetic flux, so a changing current in one induces M di/dt in the other.
It scales with loop area and matters most for low-impedance victims and long parallel runs. Fourth, radiation, where energy propagates through space, which is the same as EMI.

To prevent it, I attack whichever side is cheapest: increase separation or shield for capacitive; shrink loops and use planes for inductive; give each circuit its own return, add decoupling and use planes for common impedance; slow the aggressor's edges; lower the victim's impedance or use differential signalling; and filter.
The 3 watts spacing rule and ground guards help crosstalk."
